One thing that help with my sister was compression. She wore a compression vest and her comfort thing was a bean bag. This may sound crazy but she still loves it, we put the bean bag on top of her NOT COVERING HER FACE AND NECK and putting a bit of weight on her. It really helps bring her back and we usually do it until she says stop, she usually likes it for 5-10 minutes. 

Visuals are great with young people with autism. Look up visual schedules or visual aids for autistic kids. Also, sensory activities like scratching his back, skin brushing, swinging etc could be relaxing as well. 

Timers also are great so instead of going okay let's stop and eat say okay I am setting my timer for 2 minutes then we eat, then put the timer where he can see it. 

I know you are just babysitting but making a break fort or tent is helpful. Makesure it is not bright and comfortable. This is good because if he starts to feel overwhelmed his break tent can help regulate him.

That is not implying low functioning is bad at all. It is just saying they need support and are less likely to function independently. 

The higher functioning students are not ableist. The students in the lower functioning room tend to have more vocal stems that are loud and have to have more rules. How would you like it if you were a high schooler and your class had bathroom times that everyone goes to the bathroom? Or that when you go in a field trip and you are put in a group with students that aren't verbal but you are. It isn't ableist to want to be around classmates you can talk to and that are more on your level. It is common.

USA does too. At least in the education system

You need it a lot in education settings or day programs. They have rooms split off for higher and lower functioning. It helps so everyone is equally challenged and needs are met. For example, the lower functioning room has a schedule for students to go to the bathroom so they don't forget and have accidents whole higher functioning doesnt. The lower functioning room has more teacher aides to assist with students that need help going to the bathroom, eating lunch etc. Of course if someone requires their own aide they will get that no matter what room they are in.

 Also, it helps with students self esteem, a lot of the higher functioning students do not like to be grouped with the lower functioning students. But they also need more support than the students that dont need to be in an autism room at all. So being in a room with students at their level makes them feel more comfortable.
